modules.title: Module 4: Association Rule Analysis and Advanced Data Mining
modules.subtitle: PECST525 | Data Mining

children.title: Association Rule Concepts
children.body:
Introduction

Association rule mining finds interesting relationships among items in large transactional data sets. It is the classic “market-basket” problem: which products are bought together?

Basic Definitions

  • Let I = {i1, i2, …, im} be a set of items, and D a set of transactions where each transaction is a subset of I.
  • An itemset is a set of one or more items. A k-itemset contains k items.
  • An association rule has the form X → Y, where X and Y are disjoint itemsets (X ∩ Y = ∅). X is the antecedent, Y the consequent.
  • Support of X → Y is the fraction of transactions containing X ∪ Y: support(X ∪ Y) = count(X ∪ Y) / |D|.
  • Confidence of X → Y is the fraction of transactions containing X that also contain Y: confidence = support(X ∪ Y) / support(X).

Frequent Itemsets

An itemset whose support is at least a user-specified minimum support is a frequent itemset. A rule is strong if its confidence is at least a minimum confidence. Mining has two steps:

  1. Find all frequent itemsets (the expensive step).
  2. Generate strong association rules from those itemsets.

Example

Transactions:

TIDItems
T1bread, milk
T2bread, diapers, beer, eggs
T3milk, diapers, beer, cola
T4bread, milk, diapers, beer
T5bread, milk, diapers, cola

For the rule {bread, milk} → {diapers}: support = 2/5 = 40%, confidence = 2/3 ≈ 66.7%.

Interestingness

  • Support shows how often a rule applies; confidence shows how reliable it is.
  • A rule can have high confidence but low support (rare, unreliable) or high support but low confidence.
  • Lift = confidence / support(Y) corrects for independent items: lift > 1 means positive correlation.
  • Rules are filtered by both thresholds; additional interestingness measures (lift, chi-square, conviction) remove redundant or spurious rules.

Applications

  • Market-basket analysis, product placement and cross-selling.
  • Recommender systems and web click-stream analysis.
  • Medical diagnosis (symptom → disease associations).
  • Fraud detection and network intrusion patterns.

Exam Tip

Define support and confidence with formulas first, then compute both for a small rule.

children.title: Apriori Algorithm
children.body:
Idea

Apriori is the classic level-wise algorithm for finding frequent itemsets. It uses the Apriori property (anti-monotonicity): if an itemset is frequent, all its subsets are frequent; equivalently, if an itemset is infrequent, all its supersets are infrequent. This lets the algorithm prune candidates without scanning the database.

Algorithm

  1. Scan D and count 1-itemsets; keep those with support ≥ min_sup (L1).
  2. Join: generate candidate k-itemsets (Ck) by joining pairs of (k−1)-itemsets in Lk−1 that share their first k−2 items.
  3. Prune: delete any candidate in Ck that contains an infrequent (k−1)-subset.
  4. Count support of the remaining candidates by scanning D, and keep those ≥ min_sup (Lk).
  5. Repeat steps 2–4 until no candidate itemsets remain.
  6. Generate rules from each frequent itemset and keep those with confidence ≥ min_conf.
L1 = frequent 1-itemsets
for k = 2, 3, ... while Lk-1 is not empty:
    Ck = apriori_gen(Lk-1)      // join + prune
    count support of Ck in D
    Lk = candidates with support >= min_sup
return union of all Lk

Worked Example (min_sup = 2, min_conf = 50%)

Using the five transactions from the previous note:

L1: bread 4, milk 4, diapers 4, beer 3, cola 2
    (eggs 1 is pruned)

C2 candidates and counts:
  {bread, milk}      3  -> frequent
  {bread, diapers}   3  -> frequent
  {bread, beer}      2  -> frequent
  {milk, diapers}    3  -> frequent
  {milk, beer}       2  -> frequent
  {milk, cola}       2  -> frequent
  {diapers, beer}    3  -> frequent
  {diapers, cola}    2  -> frequent
  {bread, cola}      1  -> pruned
  {beer, cola}       1  -> pruned

L3: {bread, milk, diapers}    2
    {bread, diapers, beer}    2
    {milk, diapers, beer}     2
    {milk, diapers, cola}     2

C4: {bread, milk, diapers, beer} 1 -> pruned
L4 is empty, so the algorithm stops.

Generating Rules

From {bread, milk, diapers} (support 2/5 = 40%):

RuleSupportConfidence
bread → milk, diapers40%2/4 = 50%
milk → bread, diapers40%2/4 = 50%
bread, milk → diapers40%2/3 = 66.7%
diapers → bread, milk40%2/4 = 50%

All four satisfy min_conf = 50%.

Advantages

  • Simple and easy to implement.
  • Uses the anti-monotone property to prune the search space effectively.
  • Produces all frequent itemsets, not just the top ones.

Limitations

  • Multiple database scans (one per level) - expensive for large data.
  • Candidate generation can be huge, especially for dense or long transactions.
  • Rarely used as-is for very large data; FP-Growth and parallel variants are preferred.
  • Sensitive to the choice of min_sup: too high misses rules, too low explodes the candidate set.

Exam Tip

Show the level-wise tables (C1 → L1 → C2 → L2 → C3 …) and state the anti-monotone property in words.

children.title: FP Growth Algorithm
children.body:
Idea

FP-Growth (Frequent Pattern Growth) mines frequent itemsets without candidate generation. It compresses the database into an FP-tree and then recursively mines that tree, which is much faster than Apriori on large or dense data.

Two Main Steps

  1. Build the FP-tree: scan the database once to count item frequencies, discard infrequent items, order remaining items in each transaction by descending frequency, then insert each transaction into a prefix tree that shares common prefixes.
  2. Mine the tree: for each frequent item (processed from least to most frequent), build its conditional pattern base and conditional FP-tree, then recurse.

FP-Tree Structure

  • The root is a null node; each other node holds an item, a count and a pointer to its parent/children.
  • A header table stores each frequent item, its support count and a link to the first node of that item.
  • Common prefixes are shared, so the tree is much smaller than the original database.

Example (min_sup = 2)

Transactions ordered by descending frequency (diapers, bread, milk, beer, cola):

T1: bread, milk                     -> bread, milk
T2: bread, diapers, beer, eggs       -> diapers, bread, beer
T3: milk, diapers, beer, cola        -> diapers, milk, beer, cola
T4: bread, milk, diapers, beer       -> diapers, bread, milk, beer
T5: bread, milk, diapers, cola       -> diapers, bread, milk, cola

Resulting FP-tree:

                 null
              /         \
      diapers:4        bread:1
      /       \             \
bread:3     milk:1        milk:1
  |           |
beer:1      beer:1
  |           |
milk:2      cola:1
 /    \
beer:1  cola:1

Conditional Pattern Base Example

For item cola, the paths ending at cola are:

diapers, bread, milk : 1
diapers, milk, beer  : 1

The conditional FP-tree for cola contains {diapers:2, milk:2, bread:1, beer:1}. With min_sup = 2 the frequent conditional items are diapers and milk, giving the frequent itemset {diapers, milk, cola} with support 2 - the same result Apriori found.

Apriori vs FP-Growth

AspectAprioriFP-Growth
Candidate generationYes (join + prune)None
Database scansOne per levelTwo (count, build tree)
Data structureItemset listsFP-tree
Speed on dense dataSlowMuch faster
MemoryLowerHigher (stores the tree)

Advantages

  • No candidate generation.
  • Fewer database scans.
  • Very efficient for dense data sets.

Limitations

  • The FP-tree can be large when transactions do not share prefixes.
  • Building and mining the tree can be memory-intensive.
  • The implementation is more complex than Apriori.

Exam Tip

Draw a small FP-tree and one conditional pattern base; mention that no candidates are generated.

children.title: Web Content Mining
children.body:
Introduction

Web content mining extracts useful information from the content of web pages - text, HTML structure, images, audio and video. The content is largely unstructured or semi-structured, which makes it harder than mining relational data.

What Is Mined

  • Text: paragraphs, headings, lists and tables.
  • Semi-structured markup: HTML/XML tags, links and metadata.
  • Multimedia: images, audio and video (with feature extraction).

Main Approaches

ApproachDescription
Information retrieval (IR)Rank documents by relevance to a query
Text mining / NLPTokenise, classify, cluster and summarise text
Wrapper inductionLearn extraction rules for structured records from pages
Web page summarisationProduce a compact representation of a page or site
Topic / concept discoveryGroup pages by latent topics or concepts

Challenges

  • Enormous volume and rapid change of web content.
  • Unstructured text with noise, boilerplate, ads and navigation.
  • Heterogeneous formats and encodings.
  • Duplicate and near-duplicate pages.
  • Privacy and copyright concerns.

Applications

  • Search engines and vertical search.
  • News aggregation and topic tracking.
  • Opinion and sentiment analysis on reviews and social media.
  • Product and price comparison by extracting offers.
  • E-learning and digital libraries.

Exam Tip

Contrast content mining (what the page says) with structure mining (how pages link) and usage mining (how users behave).

children.title: Web Structure Mining and PageRank
children.body:
Introduction

Web structure mining analyses the hyperlink graph of the web: pages are nodes and hyperlinks are directed edges. Link structure reveals authority and relevance that page text alone cannot show.

The Web as a Graph

  • In-degree: number of links pointing to a page (a popularity signal).
  • Out-degree: number of links leaving a page.
  • The graph is huge, sparse and constantly changing, with hubs, authorities and link farms.

PageRank

PageRank (Brin and Page, used by Google) assigns each page a score based on the number and quality of links to it: a link from an important page is worth more than a link from an unimportant one.

PR(A) = (1 − d) + d × Σ PR(Ti) / C(Ti)
          i in In(A)

d     = damping factor (typically 0.85)
In(A) = pages linking to A
C(Ti) = number of out-links from page Ti

The scores are computed iteratively over the whole graph until they converge.

Worked Example

Three pages: A links to B and C; B links to C; C links to A. With d = 0.85 and starting PR = 1 for every page:

PR(A) = 0.15 + 0.85 × PR(C)/1
PR(B) = 0.15 + 0.85 × PR(A)/2
PR(C) = 0.15 + 0.85 × (PR(A)/2 + PR(B)/1)

After a few iterations the values converge, with C receiving
contributions from both A and B and therefore scoring highest.

HITS (Hubs and Authorities)

  • A hub is a page that links to many good authorities; an authority is a page linked to by many good hubs.
  • Hubs and authorities are computed mutually: good hubs point to good authorities, and good authorities are pointed to by good hubs.
  • HITS is query-dependent; PageRank is query-independent.

PageRank vs HITS

AspectPageRankHITS
ScopeWhole web graphA small subgraph for a query
Score typeSingle importance scoreTwo scores (hub, authority)
ComputationIterative, offlineIterative, per query
CostHigh but cachedRepeated per query

Exam Tip

Write the PageRank formula, explain the damping factor, and say that scores are computed iteratively.

children.title: Web Usage Mining - Preprocessing and Data Structures
children.body:
Introduction

Web usage mining discovers patterns in how users interact with websites, using data recorded in web server logs, proxy logs, browser logs and application data.

Data Sources

  • Server logs: IP address, timestamp, URL, method, status, referrer, user agent, bytes.
  • Proxy logs: requests from many users through a shared proxy.
  • Client-side data: cookies, JavaScript events, browser history.
  • Application data: purchases, registrations and other business events.

Preprocessing Steps

  1. Data cleaning: remove irrelevant requests (images, scripts, failed responses, robot traffic).
  2. User identification: identify distinct users using IP, cookies, login ids and heuristics.
  3. Session identification: split each user’s requests into sessions using a timeout or a navigation-based rule.
  4. Pageview identification: group requests that belong to one page (frames, embedded resources).
  5. Path completion: infer missing page requests, e.g. pages reached through the browser cache or the Back button.
  6. Data integration and transformation: merge with site structure and content, then format for mining.

Preprocessing Challenges

  • Shared IP addresses hide different users behind a proxy or NAT.
  • Caching means some page requests never reach the server.
  • Robots and spiders create artificial requests.
  • Session boundaries are ambiguous without explicit login or timeouts.

Data Structures for Mining

StructureDescription
GraphPages as nodes and links followed as edges; supports path analysis
User × page matrixRows are users/sessions, columns are pages, cells are visits or times
Page × page matrixCo-visitation counts for association and similarity
Data cubeUsage aggregated by time, user, page, region for OLAP

Exam Tip

List the preprocessing steps in order (cleaning → user → session → pageview → path completion), then name one data structure.

children.title: Web Usage Mining - Pattern Discovery and Pattern Analysis
children.body:
Pattern Discovery

After preprocessing, usage data is mined for behavioural patterns.

  • Statistical analysis: frequency, average visit time, top pages, error rates.
  • Association rules: pages frequently visited together (e.g. product → accessory).
  • Clustering: group users with similar browsing behaviour, or pages with similar usage.
  • Classification: predict user type or future behaviour from labelled sessions.
  • Sequential patterns: frequent navigation paths, e.g. Home → Category → Product → Cart.

Pattern Analysis

Discovered patterns must be filtered, validated and presented:

  • OLAP on usage cubes: roll-up, drill-down, slice and dice over time, user and page dimensions.
  • Visualisation: navigation graphs, heat maps and path diagrams.
  • Knowledge filtering: remove trivial or redundant patterns and apply domain constraints.

Frequent Traversal Paths and Association Rules

A frequent traversal path is a sequence of pages followed by many users; an association rule relates pages visited together. Both help restructure navigation and recommend content.

Example sequential patterns:
Home -> Products -> Product -> Cart -> Checkout
Home -> Search -> Product -> Reviews

Applications

  • Personalisation and adaptive websites.
  • Recommender systems and targeted promotions.
  • Site redesign, cache and prefetch policy.
  • Detecting abnormal behaviour (bots, attacks).
  • Measuring campaign effectiveness.

Challenges

  • Privacy and consent.
  • Incomplete logs due to caching and proxies.
  • Session ambiguity and robot traffic.
  • Large scale and evolving site structure.

Exam Tip

Give one example for each discovered pattern type: path, association and cluster.

children.title: Text Data Analysis and Information Retrieval
children.body:
Introduction

Text mining discovers useful patterns and knowledge from unstructured text. Information retrieval (IR) is the related problem of finding documents relevant to a user query. Both operate on natural-language data rather than on neatly structured tables.

Text Preprocessing

  1. Tokenisation: split text into words or terms.
  2. Stop-word removal: delete very common words such as “the”, “is”, “and”.
  3. Stemming / lemmatisation: reduce inflected words to their base form (e.g. “studies” → “studi” / “study”).
  4. Normalisation: case folding, handling numbers, dates and punctuation.
  5. Feature selection: keep informative terms (TF-IDF, chi-square) to reduce dimensionality.

Document Representation

  • Bag of words: a document is a set (or multiset) of terms, ignoring order.
  • Term vector: each term has a weight, often TF-IDF.
  • Probabilistic model: terms follow a distribution estimated from the collection.
  • Embeddings: dense vectors learned by neural models capture semantics.

Information Retrieval Problem

Given a query q and a collection of documents D, return the documents most relevant to q, ranked by relevance. Unlike a database query, the result is approximate and the “correct” answer is not a set-theoretic match.

Database Query vs IR

AspectDatabase queryInformation retrieval
DataStructured recordsUnstructured text
MatchingExact / deterministicApproximate / ranked
ResultAll matching tuplesRanked list of documents
CorrectnessPreciseJudged by relevance

Text Mining Tasks

  • Document classification (spam, topic, sentiment).
  • Document clustering and topic discovery.
  • Information extraction (entities, relations).
  • Summarisation and keyword extraction.
  • Association and sequence mining over terms or documents.

Applications

  • Search engines and enterprise search.
  • Recommender systems and news feeds.
  • Opinion mining on reviews and social media.
  • Medical and legal document analysis.

Exam Tip

State the IR problem precisely and contrast it with a database query; both are standard short-answer questions.

children.title: Basic Measures for Text Retrieval
children.body:
Introduction

Retrieval quality is measured against a known set of relevant documents. The confusion table below is the basis of all standard measures.

Contingency Table

RetrievedNot retrieved
RelevantTrue Positive (TP)False Negative (FN)
Not relevantFalse Positive (FP)True Negative (TN)

Measures

Precision = TP / (TP + FP)    fraction of retrieved documents that are relevant
Recall    = TP / (TP + FN)    fraction of relevant documents that were retrieved
F-measure = 2 × P × R / (P + R)    harmonic mean
Accuracy  = (TP + TN) / (TP + TN + FP + FN)

Worked Example

A search returns 20 documents, of which 12 are relevant (TP = 12, FP = 8). The collection has 30 relevant documents in total, so FN = 18.

Precision = 12/20 = 0.60
Recall    = 12/30 = 0.40
F1        = 2(0.60)(0.40)/(0.60+0.40) = 0.48

Precision–Recall Trade-off

  • Returning more documents raises recall but usually lowers precision.
  • A precision–recall curve plots the trade-off; the break-even point is where precision equals recall.
  • The F-measure combines them; F1 weights precision and recall equally.
  • For ranked retrieval, measures at cut-off k (precision@k, recall@k) and mean average precision (MAP) are common.

Other Measures

MeasureMeaning
Precision@kRelevant documents among the top k results
MAPMean of average precision across queries
MRRMean reciprocal rank of the first relevant result
NDCGRanking quality with graded relevance

Exam Tip

Draw the 2 × 2 table, write precision and recall, and compute them for the numbers given.

children.title: Text Retrieval Methods
children.body:
Approaches

Retrieval models rank documents by how well they match a query.

ModelKey ideaNote
BooleanDocument matches if the Boolean query is trueNo ranking; simple but rigid
Vector spaceDocuments and query are TF-IDF vectors; rank by cosine similarityMost classical model
ProbabilisticEstimate P(relevant | document); BM25 is a practical variantStrong baseline
Language modelRank by P(query | document model)Needs smoothing
Latent semanticProject terms and documents to a low-rank spaceCaptures synonymy

Boolean Model

A query is built with AND, OR and NOT; a document is retrieved if it satisfies the expression. No ranking is produced, so users often get too many or too few results.

Vector Space Model

Each document and the query become a vector over the term vocabulary. Weights are TF-IDF: term frequency in the document × inverse document frequency in the collection.

tf-idf(t, d) = tf(t, d) × log(N / df(t))
cosine(q, d) = (q · d) / (||q|| × ||d||)

Relevance is the cosine of the angle between the vectors: closer direction means higher similarity.

TF-IDF Intuition

  • A term frequent in one document is important for that document (high tf).
  • A term frequent across all documents is not discriminative (low idf).
  • Multiplying the two rewards terms that are both frequent locally and rare globally.

Probabilistic Model and BM25

The probabilistic model estimates the probability that a document is relevant to the query. BM25 refines this with term saturation and document-length normalisation, and is a strong default in modern search engines.

Comparison

  • Boolean: exact matching, no ranking, easy to implement.
  • Vector space: ranking via cosine, intuitive, but assumes term independence.
  • Probabilistic: principled ranking (BM25), still assumes independence.
  • Language model: well-founded, needs smoothing to handle unseen terms.
  • LSI / embeddings: capture synonymy and context at higher computational cost.

Exam Tip

Compare Boolean, vector space and probabilistic models in a table; know that cosine similarity and TF-IDF belong to the vector space model.

children.title: Text Indexing Techniques
children.body:
Why Index?

Scanning every document for each query is far too slow for large collections. An index maps query terms to the documents that contain them, so retrieval touches only relevant postings.

Inverted Index

For each term, store a postings list of the documents (and optionally positions) where it occurs.

Term        Postings (doc : tf)
bread       1:2, 2:1, 4:1, 5:1
milk        1:1, 3:1, 4:1, 5:1
diapers     2:1, 3:1, 4:1, 5:1
beer        2:1, 3:1, 4:1

Building the Index

  1. Tokenise each document and assign term ids.
  2. Collect (term, document) pairs.
  3. Sort pairs by term.
  4. Merge to form postings lists and write the dictionary.

Dictionary and Postings

  • The dictionary stores each term and a pointer to its postings; implemented as a hash table, B-tree or trie.
  • Postings are usually stored on disk in sorted order and compressed.
  • Positional indexes keep term positions, enabling phrase and proximity queries at extra storage cost.

Compression and Speed-ups

  • Delta encoding: store gaps between document ids rather than absolute ids.
  • Variable-byte / gamma codes: encode small numbers in fewer bits.
  • Skip pointers: jump ahead in postings lists to speed up intersections.

Answering Queries

Boolean AND intersects postings lists; OR merges them; phrase queries use positional postings to check adjacency. Ranking models then score the retrieved candidates with TF-IDF or BM25.

Exam Tip

Draw a small inverted index for three documents and demonstrate an AND query by intersecting postings lists.

children.title: Important Definitions and Quick Revision
children.body:
Important Definitions

  • Association rule: an implication X → Y between disjoint itemsets.
  • Support: fraction of transactions containing X ∪ Y.
  • Confidence: support(X ∪ Y) / support(X).
  • Frequent itemset: an itemset with support at least the minimum support.
  • Apriori property: if an itemset is frequent, all its subsets are frequent (anti-monotone).
  • Apriori algorithm: level-wise candidate generation and pruning for frequent itemsets.
  • FP-tree: a compressed prefix tree of transactions used by FP-Growth.
  • Conditional pattern base: the set of prefix paths ending at a given item, with their counts.
  • Web content mining: extracting knowledge from the content of web pages.
  • Web structure mining: analysing the hyperlink graph of the web.
  • Web usage mining: discovering patterns in user navigation recorded in logs.
  • PageRank: an iterative link-based importance score for web pages.
  • Hub / authority: pages that link to good authorities / pages linked to by good hubs (HITS).
  • Session: a sequence of page requests by one user within a time window.
  • Path completion: inferring page requests missing from logs because of caching.
  • Text mining: discovering patterns and knowledge from unstructured text.
  • Information retrieval: finding and ranking documents relevant to a query.
  • Precision: TP / (TP + FP).
  • Recall: TP / (TP + FN).
  • F-measure: harmonic mean of precision and recall.
  • TF-IDF: term weight combining local frequency and global rarity.
  • Inverted index: a term → postings-list index for fast retrieval.
  • Positional index: an inverted index that stores term positions.

Formulas to Memorise

support(X -> Y)   = count(X ∪ Y) / |D|
confidence(X -> Y)= support(X ∪ Y) / support(X)
lift              = confidence / support(Y)
PR(A)             = (1 − d) + d Σ PR(Ti)/C(Ti)
Precision         = TP / (TP + FP)
Recall            = TP / (TP + FN)
F1                = 2PR / (P + R)
tf-idf(t,d)       = tf(t,d) × log(N / df(t))
cosine(q,d)       = (q·d) / (||q|| ||d||)

Quick Comparison Tables

Apriori vs FP-Growth

AspectAprioriFP-Growth
CandidatesGenerates and prunesNone
ScansOne per levelTwo
StructureItemset listsFP-tree
Dense dataSlowFast

Web mining types

TypeWhat is analysedExample
ContentPage text and markupSentiment analysis, extraction
StructureHyperlink graphPageRank, HITS
UsageLogs of user behaviourFrequent paths, recommendations

Retrieval models

ModelRanking?Core idea
BooleanNoLogical matching
Vector spaceYesTF-IDF + cosine
Probabilistic / BM25YesP(relevance) with saturation
Language modelYesP(query | document)

Likely Long-Answer Questions

  1. Define support and confidence and explain association rule mining with an example.
  2. Explain the Apriori algorithm with the level-wise candidate tables.
  3. Explain FP-Growth and draw the FP-tree for a small data set.
  4. Compare Apriori and FP-Growth.
  5. Explain web content, structure and usage mining.
  6. Explain PageRank with its formula and an example.
  7. Explain the preprocessing steps of web usage mining.
  8. Explain pattern discovery and pattern analysis in web usage mining.
  9. Explain information retrieval and the measures precision, recall and F-measure.
  10. Compare Boolean, vector space and probabilistic retrieval models.
  11. Explain inverted indexes and how an AND query is answered.

Important Short-Answer Questions

  1. Define association rule.
  2. Define support and confidence.
  3. What is a frequent itemset?
  4. State the Apriori property.
  5. What is an FP-tree?
  6. What is lift?

Study Strategy

  • Practise the Apriori level-wise tables on a small transaction set.
  • Draw one FP-tree and one conditional pattern base.
  • Memorise the PageRank formula and explain the damping factor in one sentence.
